questiontext.text: Within each alignment, in which direction does Boyer-Moore compare the pattern against the text?

answer.text: Right to left (from the end of the pattern toward the front)

feedback.text: Correct — matching from the rightmost pattern character enables large skips.

answer.text: Left to right

feedback.text: No — that is KMP; Boyer-Moore compares right to left.

answer.text: From the middle outward

feedback.text: No — Boyer-Moore starts at the rightmost character.

answer.text: In random order

feedback.text: No — comparison order is fixed: right to left.

generalfeedback.text: Boyer-Moore aligns the pattern and compares from its last character backward, which is what makes its heuristics able to skip.

questiontext.text: Which two heuristics does classic Boyer-Moore use to decide how far to shift the pattern?

answer.text: Bad-character and good-suffix

feedback.text: Correct — these two rules determine the shift distance.

answer.text: Failure function and rolling hash

feedback.text: No — those belong to KMP and Rabin-Karp respectively.

answer.text: Bad-character and rolling hash

feedback.text: No — the rolling hash is Rabin-Karp, not Boyer-Moore.

answer.text: Good-suffix and binary search

feedback.text: No — Boyer-Moore does not use binary search.

generalfeedback.text: Boyer-Moore combines the bad-character heuristic and the good-suffix heuristic, taking the larger shift of the two.

questiontext.text: Why is Boyer-Moore often described as sublinear in practice?

answer.text: Its heuristics let it skip many text characters without inspecting them, best case around O(n/m)

feedback.text: Correct — large skips mean it can examine far fewer than n characters.

answer.text: It uses a hash to test all windows in O(1)

feedback.text: No — that is Rabin-Karp; Boyer-Moore skips via heuristics.

answer.text: It sorts the text first to enable binary search

feedback.text: No — Boyer-Moore does not sort or binary-search.

answer.text: It never needs to preprocess the pattern

feedback.text: No — it does preprocess to build its heuristic tables.

generalfeedback.text: On large alphabets and long patterns, skips are large, so Boyer-Moore inspects far fewer than n characters — best case ~O(n/m). This is why grep uses it.

questiontext.text: The Boyer-Moore rule that shifts the pattern based on the mismatched text character is called the ______-character heuristic. Give the missing word.

answer.text: bad

feedback.text: Correct — the bad-character heuristic.

answer.text: bad*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: When does Boyer-Moore tend to shine most?

answer.text: Searching a long pattern over a large alphabet, where average-case skipping is largest

feedback.text: Correct — big alphabets and long patterns produce the biggest skips.

answer.text: When you need a strict worst-case linear guarantee out of the box

feedback.text: No — naive Boyer-Moore is O(nm); KMP gives the built-in linear guarantee.

answer.text: When searching for many patterns at once

feedback.text: No — multi-pattern search favors Rabin-Karp.

answer.text: When the pattern is a single character

feedback.text: No — with m = 1 there is little to skip; Boyer-Moore's advantage shrinks.

generalfeedback.text: Boyer-Moore is fastest in practice for long patterns and large alphabets, which is why tools like grep use it.

questiontext.text: The naive Boyer-Moore (bad-character only) can degrade to O(n × m) in the worst case, but adding the Galil rule restores O(n + m).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — worst case is O(nm) naively; the Galil rule gives a linear guarantee.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — the naive worst case really is O(nm), and the Galil rule really does bound it to O(n + m).

questiontext.text: Boyer-Moore is a common choice for fast text search tools such as grep.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — its sublinear average behavior makes it a practical favorite.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — Boyer-Moore variants are indeed widely used in tools like grep.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Boyer-Moore are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Longer patterns and larger alphabets tend to make it faster (bigger skips)

feedback.text: Yes — more distinctive characters allow larger shifts.

answer.text: It compares characters from the right end of the pattern first

feedback.text: Yes — right-to-left comparison is central to the method.

answer.text: It guarantees O(n + m) time without any extra rule

feedback.text: No — the naive version is O(nm); linearity needs the Galil rule.

answer.text: It uses a rolling hash to compare windows

feedback.text: No — the rolling hash is Rabin-Karp, not Boyer-Moore.

generalfeedback.text: Boyer-Moore: right-to-left comparison, faster with long patterns/large alphabets, but only linear with the Galil rule; rolling hashes belong to Rabin-Karp.
